# **Serious Game Project: MVP Design Document**

You've identified your topic, tested three different game perspectives, and playtested with real players. Now you're going to document your game in detail before you build it digitally. This design document is your blueprint. It shows what your game looks like, how it works, and why each part matters.

Your design document should have:

* A clear description of your chosen paper prototype  
* Sketches and descriptions of your game screens and mechanics  
* Justification for why this design serves your learning goal

---

## **Part 1 \- Your Game at a Glance**

**Sentence 1:** We are making a game about \[topic\] for \[audience\], because they are the people who most need to understand it.

| We are making a game about the migration of grey whales for everyone because they are the people who most need to understand it.  |
| :---- |

**Sentence 2:** We want a player to walk away understanding \[one specific thing\]. 

| We want a player to walk away understanding the effect of climate change and pollution on aquatic wildlife.  |
| :---- |

## **Part 2 \- Choose Your Paper Prototype**

**Choose (and refine) your best paper prototype. Add pictures of it here:**

| ![][image1]  |
| :---- |

**Describe how to play your paper prototype.**

| There is trash and food scattered around, the trash/fishing boats and food increase/decrease health hearts. There are mystery “foods” that are either fishermen who damage heath by 2 hearts or pods of fish that increase the whales health 3 hearts. The goal is to make it to alaska without the health bar reaching zero. There is also a time rush because as the whale is traveling north to escape the heat in the summer, and if it gets too warm the number of fish decreases, making it more difficult to go north, and more likely to die.  |
| :---- |

**What made this prototype work?** Describe one moment from playtesting that showed you this was the right direction. What did a playtester do or say?

| The element of surprise and debating whether it is worth it to take the risk or play it safe.  |
| :---- |

## **Part 3 \- Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics**

These three things work together to create your game experience.

**What is your most important mechanic?** The rule or action. (Example: "The player chooses which person to help with limited time per turn.")

| The player navigates obstacles and aims for food to continue the journey to the end.  |
| :---- |

**What dynamic should this elicit?** What happens as a result? What tension or situation does the mechanic create? (Example: "The player faces real tension because they can't help everyone.")

| The player undertrands how tricky and tiring it is to navigate life as a migrating whale.  |
| :---- |

**What aesthetic should players feel?** What do you want it to feel like to play? (Example: "Stress. Moral weight. The feeling of helplessness in the face of competing needs.")

| Stress to emulate the experience that humans have caused upon whales. And also appreciation for nature and how earth was before humans intenvted plastics and starting harming aquatic life.  |
| :---- |

**How do these three work together to serve your learning goal?**

| The player will see how difficult it is to be a whale and how humans impact all life of earth, especially aquatic. |
| :---- |

---

## **Part 4 \- Mechanics and Story Alignment**

Now let’s flesh out your paper prototype into a game idea\! In a serious game, your mechanics should embody your message, not just decorate it.

**What story are you telling?** Briefly describe the scenario, the world, or the situation the player enters.

| In this scenario, the player is a solitary grey whale that is migrating along the Pacific coast, leaving the warm lagoons in Baja Mexico to go to the Bering/Chukchi seas where they can feed. |
| :---- |

**How do your mechanics embody this story?** Don't explain it through dialogue or cutscenes. Explain it through what the player actually does. Why does that specific action matter thematically?

| The player is initially introduced to the journey they are facing, and then it completes obstacles to make it to their destination. When the whale (navigated by the player) accidentally runs into danger (trash or fishing boat), their health (measured by hearts) decreases in response– which could lead to their death.  |
| :---- |

---

## **Part 5 \- Goals, Subgoals, and Pacing**

**Overall goal:** What is the player trying to accomplish? This should connect to your learning goal.

| Survive/complete the migration and gain the most possible points while leveling up |
| :---- |

**Subgoals:** What are 2-4 smaller objectives the player works toward on the way to the overall goal? (List them in order.)

| Avoid nets, trash and fish that will harm health  Collect fish before the fishing boat collects them |
| :---- |

**Pacing:** How does the game get harder or more complex? When does the player feel successful? When do they feel challenged? You can sketch a quick graph, describe it, or both.

| ![][image2] There are 10 levels, and the color of the levels gradually gradient. They start at yellow then fade to green represeenting cooling ocean temperatures as the player progresses and the increase in food/prosperity as they continue to the feeding grounds.The player feels successful when they complete each level, and most when they win the whole game. They feel challenged when they die and are forced to retry the level from the start. The starting level is very easy and introduces the game mechanics. Each level gets increasingly harder (though not specifically more complex) as the player improves keeping the game engaging and challenging.  |
| :---- |

## **Part 7 \- Sketch Your MVG**

Sketch out everything that will be needed for your “Minimum Viable Game.” Rough sketches are better than no sketches. These don't need to be pretty.

**What does the player see on screen?** Sketch the **minimum** different views for your game to work. 

| ![][image3]  |
| :---- |

**What are the UI elements?** (Player character, enemies, items, obstacles, buttons, counters, timers, text, icons, etc. What’s the **minimum** that the player would need to see and interact with?)

| Shipping boats (obstacle \-1 heart) Fish (food/points) Trash (obstacle \-1 heart) Nets (obstacle \-1 heart) Larger fishing boat (competing with whale) Point score 5 Hearts  Text (providing information) Grey whale (player character) |
| :---- |

**How does the game communicate?** How does the player know what happened? (Visual feedback, sounds, text, numbers, images?)

| Point total communicated in numbers Text to provide information  Visual feedback and images is the largest way the gameplay is communicated  Hearts as image to indicate life levels  |
